nameStory: The seaside lady beetle gets its common name from its coastal lifestyle, making its home along beaches, salt marshes, and bay islands where few other lady beetles dare to venture. Unlike its garden-dwelling cousins, this hardy beetle has adapted to the salty, windy conditions right at the ocean's edge. It's truly a beach lover in the lady beetle world!
description: The seaside lady beetle is a sturdy, oval-shaped lady beetle that calls New England's coastal areas home. At 4-6.7mm long, it's on the larger side for lady beetles, with a body that can range from light brown and yellow to bright orange or red. What makes it distinctive are its large black spots that often connect along the sides, plus a prominent black spot (sometimes split in two) right in the center of its pronotum - that's the shield-like section just behind its head. This is the only species in its genus, making it quite special among North American lady beetles.

idTips.label: Connected side spots
idTips.description: Look for large black spots that merge or connect along the beetle's sides, creating a distinctive chain-like pattern that feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Central pronotum spot
idTips.description: The shield behind the head has one large central black spot (occasionally split into two) that stands out prominently against the lighter background

idTips.label: Coastal habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in salty coastal environments - if you're seeing it inland, it's probably a different species

idTips.label: Elongated oval shape
idTips.description: The body is noticeably more oval and elongated than the typical round lady beetle shape, feeling substantial and robust when gently handled

idTips.label: Variable coloration
idTips.description: Body color ranges from pale yellow-brown to bright orange or red, often with a slightly matte finish rather than the glossy shine of many lady beetles

habitat: In New England, look for seaside lady beetles exclusively in coastal environments like sandy beaches, salt marshes, and barrier islands. They thrive in the challenging conditions where salt spray reaches, among beach grasses, seaside goldenrod, and other salt-tolerant plants. You won't find them in inland gardens or forests - they're true specialists of the land-sea border.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active as coastal temperatures warm. Look for them crawling on beach vegetation and driftwood.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, feeding and mating among salt marsh plants and beach grasses during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, preparing for winter by seeking shelter under debris or in protected crevices near the shore.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden under driftwood, rocks, or dense vegetation near the coast, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This tough little beetle is one of the few lady beetles that can actually drink seawater and survive - it has special adaptations that let it process salt that would kill most other insects, making it a true marine specialist in a family known for garden living!
confusionNotes: Often confused with the much more common spotted pink ladybeetle, but the seaside lady beetle's spots connect along the sides while the pink ladybeetle's spots stay separate. Memory trick: "Seaside spots stick together like sand castles, pink spots stand alone like polka dots."
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Naemia, the seaside lady beetle is quite unique. When compared to other lady beetles in New England, it's most similar to the spotted pink ladybeetle, but the seaside species is larger, has connecting side spots, and is found only in coastal areas. Most other lady beetles are smaller, rounder, and prefer inland gardens and fields where salt spray never reaches.
